Background Self-report measures indicate that Yoga practices are perceived to reduce stress; however, molecular mechanisms through which YB affects stress are just beginning to be understood. While invasive sampling such as blood has been widely used to measure biological indicators such as pro-inflammatory biomarkers, the use of saliva to measure changes in various biomolecules has been increasingly recognized. As Yoga practice stimulates salivary secretion, and saliva is considered a source of biomarkers, changes in salivary cytokines before and after Yogic breathing exercise as specified in an ancient Tamil script, Thirumanthiram, were examined using a Cytokine Multiplex to compare to Attention Control (AC) group. Methods Twenty healthy volunteers were randomized into two groups stratified by gender ( N = 10 per YB and AC groups); The YB group performed two YB exercises, each for ten minutes, for a total of twenty minutes in a single session as directed by a trained Yoga instructor. The AC group read a text of their choice for 20 min. Saliva was collected immediately after YB training at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 min and analyzed by Multiplex enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Results The levels of interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-8, and monocyte chemotactic protein −1 (MCP-1) were significantly reduced in YB group when compared to AC group. The level of reduction of IL-8 was significant at all time points tested, whereas IL-1β showed reduction at 15 and 20 min time points ( p < 0.05), and MCP-1 level was marginally different at 5–20 min. There were no significant differences between YB and AC groups in the salivary levels of IL-1RA, IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, IP-10, MIP-1b, and TNF-α. Conclusions These data are the first to demonstrate the feasibility of detecting salivary cytokines using multiplex assay in response to a Yoga practice. This study was registered in Clinical Trials.gov # NCT02108769. Keywords Yoga Yogic breathing Thirumanthiram Pranayama Salivary biomarkers Cytokines Multiplex Pro-inflammatory Stress Tamil South Carolina Clinical and Translational Research UL1 RR029882 and UL1 TR000062 Balasubramanian Sundaravadivel Pure Action Inc, Texas issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2016 Background Pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines are implicated in several diseases and therefore are potential targets for molecular therapy. While non-pharmacological methods of stress reduction have long been in practice among several cultures, recently such practices are gaining acceptance worldwide. Translating information on stress reduction from ancient cultures into modern scientific literature is important to preserve and propagate such wellness practices [ 1 ]. Thirumanthiram is an ancient Tamil text written by Saint Thirumoolar who was contemporary to Saint Patanjali [ 2 , 3 ]. Thirumanthiram ( Thiru means holy or sacred or noble, manthiram means chant or mantra or hymn or sutra ) consists of over 3000 poems referring to various practices including Ethics, Devotion, and Yoga. In this anthology there are 14 poems (Numbers 564 through 577) dedicated to the practice of Yogic Breathing (YB, Pranayamam or Pranayama ). These 14 poems speak in depth about the benefits of YB and explain how breathing is an important connection between mind and body. YB is one of the several practices within the broad field of Yoga and is known to cause key changes within mind and body including blood pressure reduction, heart rate variability changes, and breathing frequency reductions [ 4 ], predominant abdominal/diaphragmatic breathing [ 5 – 7 ], improved cognitive functions (e.g., mental alertness and reduced cognitive failure) [ 8 , 9 ], increased bimanual dexterity and visuo-motor co-ordination [ 10 ], stress and symptom reduction in diseases such as cancer [ 11 ]. Behavioral practices such as relaxation and exercise could bring about meaningful molecular changes among practitioners [ 12 , 13 ]. Although Yoga practitioners from various schools widely practice YB, the techniques specified by Thirumoolar have not yet been studied for their physiological effects or changes in biomarkers. This study focused on the YB exercise specified in Poem 568 of Thirumanthiram (named Thirumoolar Pranayamam, TMP) that includes an inhalation ( Purakam ), breath-holding ( Kumbakam ), and exhalation ( Resakam ) for specified time periods [ 3 ]. To measure the changes in physiological responses to TMP, saliva was used to measure biomarkers. Saliva is an easily accessed non-invasive biologic sample rich in various biomarkers including proteins, peptides, metabolites, mRNA, DNA, lipids, and miRNA [ 14 – 18 ]. We recently reported that the practice of TMP increases salivary nerve growth factor [ 19 ], and caused wide range alteration to salivary proteome [ 20 ]. Based on the ability of YB to reduce stress and because salivary biomarkers could be utilized to assess stress, it was hypothesized that the practice of TMP would reduce the salivary expression of pro-inflammatory biomarkers. The results indicate that YB practice as specified in Thirumanthiram in fact reduced some of the key biomarkers implicated in stress and inflammation. Identification of molecular changes in easily accessible saliva could increase the ability of correlating subjective responses with biochemical measures in clinical trials involving Yoga and other mind-body practices.

extracted_data.document_summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial investigated the immediate effects of a single 20-minute Yogic Breathing (YB) session, specifically Thirumoolar Pranayamam from the ancient Tamil script Thirumanthiram, on salivary pro-inflammatory biomarkers in healthy volunteers. The study found that YB significantly reduced salivary levels of IL-1β, IL-8, and MCP-1 compared to an attention control group, with these reductions often observed at multiple time points and leading to more stable cytokine values over time.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Yogic Breathing (YB), specifically Thirumoolar Pranayamam (TMP) as described in the ancient Tamil script Thirumanthiram, which included 10 minutes of Om chanting (Pranava Pranayama) followed by 10 minutes of controlled breathing (inhale for two counts, hold for eight counts, exhale for four counts).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A single 20-minute session, consisting of two 10-minute YB exercises, was performed by the YB group. This was compared to an Attention Control group who read for 20 minutes. No dose-response comparisons were reported, and baseline cytokine levels were collected after participants learned the technique, which might affect true pre-intervention baselines.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly reduced in the Yogic Breathing (YB) group compared to the Attention Control (AC) group; reduction observed at 15 and 20 min time points (p < 0.05). Levels were diminished in the YB group even at the 0 min mark (after initial teaching). AC group levels were significantly higher than YB group at each time point. Specific quantitative data (pg/mL) is presented in supplementary materials.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Pro-inflammatory cytokine, implicated in stress and inflammation; activates cyclooxygenase-2 in the central nervous system involved in stress and pain perception; potentiates pro-inflammatory cellular processes (proliferation, migration, apoptosis, differentiation).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a single 20-minute Yogic Breathing (Thirumoolar Pranayamam) practice.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced levels indicate a reduction in stress and inflammation. Higher levels are deleterious in various diseases including cancer; considered a clinical target for autoinflammatory syndromes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Provides biochemical support for observed relaxation experience; serves as a measure of immune function and is linked to stress-related conditions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly reduced in the Yogic Breathing (YB) group compared to the Attention Control (AC) group; reduction was significant at all time points tested (0, 5, 10, 15, and 20 min post-intervention, p < 0.05). The magnitude of IL-8 reduction in the YB group was 3–6 orders lower than the AC group. Specific quantitative data (pg/mL) is presented in supplementary materials.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Pro-inflammatory chemokine, implicated in stress and inflammation; key mediator of inflammatory processes during various stress conditions involving oxidative stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a single 20-minute Yogic Breathing (Thirumoolar Pranayamam) practice.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced levels indicate a significant reduction in stress and inflammatory processes, particularly neutrophil recruitment. Elevated levels are associated with poor prognosis of breast cancer and psychosomatic disorders; regulating its level through non-pharmacological approaches like Yogic Breathing is considered important. Provides biochemical support for observed relaxation experience; serves as a measure of immune function and is linked to stress-related conditions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Marginally significantly reduced in the Yogic Breathing (YB) group compared to the Attention Control (AC) group at 5–20 min post-intervention. The YB group showed a significant reduction in MCP-1 level in saliva, whereas the AC group did not show any decline. Specific quantitative data (pg/mL) is presented in supplementary materials.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Pro-inflammatory chemokine (monocyte chemotactic protein) implicated in stress and inflammation; recruits key immune cells (monocytes, memory T cells, dendritic cells) during tissue injury or infection.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following a single 20-minute Yogic Breathing (Thirumoolar Pranayamam) practice.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests a reduction in stress-induced inflammatory processes, specifically monocyte recruitment, due to Yogic Breathing. Elevated in chronic pathological conditions; used as a biomarker for physiological dysfunctions including coronary heart disease, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety; increased levels are associated with increased severity of pathogenesis including Alzheimer’s disease (AD); a decrease could be important for the management of AD. Provides biochemical support for observed relaxation experience; serves as a measure of immune function and is linked to stress-related conditions.
